lesson_title: A Skin That Gives Itself Up
hook_text: A green gate rusting at every chip beside a grey fence untouched for forty years. Same farm, different skins.
clip_script: Rust is iron meeting oxygen and water, both. Keep them off and the metal lives. Paint is a skin: clean the steel, prime, paint, any colour, cheap. But chip it and rust starts there and creeps underneath. Galvanising is a skin of zinc from a hot dip at 450 degrees. Zinc is more eager to corrode than iron, so when you scratch it the zinc corrodes instead of the steel. It sacrifices itself. That is why the fence is fine and the gate is not. Zinc lasts decades inland, less at the salty coast, and when it is gone the red comes through. Grey only, factory only, dearer at first, but it outlives paint many times over.
visual_style: Whiteboard iron bar with oxygen and water arrows turning red; a paint skin with a chip and rust spreading beneath; a zinc skin with a scratch and the zinc edges dissolving while the steel stays grey; a timeline 5 years versus 40.
mood: Grounded and visual, like walking a farm fence line.
pacing: Rust, paint, chip, zinc, scratch, sacrifice, coast, limits.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find one painted and one galvanised steel object near your home and compare their condition.
